newsitem.title: FRANCE: France slams Commission, sees possible EU crisis.
newsitem.headline: France slams Commission, sees possible EU crisis.

text.p: France on Monday slammed the European Commission's proposals for reforming itself and said negotiations on reform of European Union institutions should be concluded at a June summit even if that meant sparking a crisis.

"We should be able to conclude in Amsterdam (on June 16-17), even if there is some turbulence and perhaps a crisis before then," European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier said in an interview with Reuters.

He said the so-called Inter-Governmental Conference (IGC) on EU reform had reached the most difficult issues, such as the future composition and role of the European Commission and reform of the weighted voting system for member states.
Barnier is France's negotiator in the IGC, which is aiming to improve the way the 15-nation Union functions to prepare for enlargement to central and eastern Europe early next century.

"Whatever their concerns or fears, the 15 must agree on what is in the Union's common interest, which is to have a real reform before enlargement. We cannot start or make a success of enlargement...without a major reform of the Union," he said.

Barnier opposed extending the IGC beyond the June summit, saying it was important to avoid colliding with other deadlines for ratifying a new treaty, selecting the first countries to join a single currency, opening enlargement negotiations and elections in several member states, including France, next year.
The Commission proposed last week that each EU state should appoint a single member of the Brussels executive in future, whereas the five larger countries now have two commissioners.
Barnier called the proposal "the worst of all solutions".
"It would be unacceptable for France to have a Commission composed of one member per country," he said.
Instead, he said France proposed the number of commissioners be limited to between 10 and 12, reflecting the real number of portfolios.
A rotation system would be written into the reformed treaty to guarantee all member states equal access to the Commission over time, he said.
"There is a risk today of having a weak Commission with too many members, a poor sharing out of responsibilities and a certain form of irresponsibility," Barnier said.
